## Contract — what goes in, what comes out

| | |
|---|---|
| **In** | the claimed ticket with its `<!-- ic:checklist -->` comment; the feature documents `/claim` read; a machine `/readiness` has verified |
| **Out** | a branch in an isolated worktree with the work committed; `.ic/checklist.md` in the worktree with every line ticked and its file and test named, and the **ticket's checklist comment updated** to match, with the head SHA; the canonical test verdict green locally |
| **Next** | `/acceptance` when the ticket has a visible surface or declares evidence; then `/open-pr` |

## When this skill starts

- **On request:** `/implement TXE-N`, "implement this ticket", "build TXE-N", "start coding".
- **From `/ic`:** as step 3, after `/claim` and `/readiness`.
- **Proactively:** the ticket has a checklist, the machine is verified, and the next step is
  code. Say "running /implement on TXE-N" and begin.
- **Not** without a checklist → `/claim` first. Not for a change with no ticket → `/lfg`.

## 1. Workspace — find out where you are before you make anything

A harness may already have put you in a linked worktree on a branch of its own, and a lane
dispatched by `/ticketing` always arrives in one. So look first, and resolve the repository's
**development branch**, which every later step reads as `$dev`: when its contract or `CLAUDE.md`
names the integration branch, `dev` is that name; when neither names one, `dev` is the
repository's default branch.

```bash
git rev-parse --show-toplevel
[ "$(git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-dir)" != "$(git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir)" ] \
  && echo "linked worktree" || echo "main checkout"
git status --porcelain
dev=$(gh repo view --json defaultBranchRef -q .defaultBranchRef.name)  # unless a contract names it
```

- **Already in a linked worktree** → start here, on this branch. Record its name; when it does
  not carry the ticket id, pass `--ticket TXE-<n>` to the tools that read it (`/handover`). Do
  not rename the branch: the harness may be tracking it. A worktree carrying someone else's
  uncommitted changes stops the run: name the changes and ask.
- **In the main checkout** → make one. Fetch the development branch, cut the ticket's branch
  from the remote's *latest* state of it, and create the worktree for that branch:

```bash
git fetch origin "$dev"
git worktree add "../<repo>-txe-<n>" -b "<handle>/txe-<n>-<slug>" "origin/$dev"
cd "../<repo>-txe-<n>"
```

- **No checkout at all** → `gh repo clone <owner>/<repo>` first, then the step above.

The branch is cut from what the remote has now. One ticket, one worktree, one branch; the
worktree and the claim comment are the ownership record. Never share a worktree between lanes.

## 2. Mirror the checklist into the worktree

`/ic`'s working directory is `.ic/` in the worktree root. Before writing anything into it,
create `.ic/.gitignore` containing `*` with the file editing tool, which keeps the directory
out of the commits. Then copy the ticket's checklist comment to
`.ic/checklist.md`.

This is the working copy; the ticket comment is the durable one. Tick here as you go, and
push the ticks back in §5.

Copy the feature folder's `Brief.md`, `Research.md` and `Tickets.md` into `.ic/` as well, when
the ticket has them. They are the reference this run works from.

Keep `.ic/progress.md` as the run's engineering log: after each requirement, each decision and
each dead end, append one line — what was done or decided, why, and what comes next. Record
what the code and the ticket do not already say: approaches tried and dropped, gotchas found,
open questions. After the context is compacted, and on every resumed entry, read the log, the
checklist and the copied documents from `.ic/` before doing anything else.

## 3. Implement — strictly, and completely

For CI pipeline creation, optimisation or modification, invoke
[ci-optimise](../ci-optimise/SKILL.md) before editing, including direct or resumed entry.
Keep its critical-path analysis and validation evidence with the checklist and current head.

For frontend work, after the workspace and checklist setup in §§1–2, invoke
[ui-text-simplify](../ui-text-simplify/SKILL.md) before editing, including direct or resumed
entry. Keep changes within the checklist and persist its affected-state checks as below.

The ticket governs; `Research.md` is earlier findings, and may be wrong or stale. Read it
Socratically — question each claim against the code as it is now — and where a better way to
deliver the ticket's requirements shows, take it: working functionality comes first.

Work the checklist, line by line. Every line becomes code **and** the test that proves it; a
requirement with no test is not done.

- **Omission.** Nothing in the checklist is skipped, deferred, stubbed with a TODO, or
  "covered by" a neighbouring change. Before §4 every box is ticked with the file and test
  that satisfies it — or the ticket has a comment saying exactly which requirement is blocked
  and why.
- **Drift.** Nothing outside the slice boundary is touched — no refactor of the neighbouring
  module, no "fix while you're in there", no widening the ticket because it would be tidier.

Follow the repository's conventions, so new code reads like the code around it; the reviewer
will. Commit in coherent steps, each message naming the requirement it satisfies (`R3: …`).
When the change needs the structure it touches reshaped first, make the change easy, then make
the easy change: the behaviour-preserving refactoring is a commit of its own, ahead of the behaviour.

Build it by software-engineering principles: high cohesion and low coupling, single
responsibility, separation of concerns, information hiding, DRY and YAGNI, honest names. Keep
these code smells out — the implementation review in §4 reads the change for them:
Mysterious Name, Duplicated Code, Feature Envy, Data Clumps, Primitive Obsession, Repeated
Switches, Shotgun Surgery, Divergent Change, Speculative Generality, Message Chains, Middle Man,
Refused Bequest. When the change creates a module or reshapes one's interface, read
[codebase-design](../codebase-design/SKILL.md) first.

If the criteria cannot be met as written, comment on the ticket with what you found and what
you propose, and wait for the LFG. That comment is the interview bank's M5 — the invalidated
assumption, its evidence and impact, and the three ways out: revise and continue, defer the
capability, or stop. It is never resolved by widening or narrowing the ticket yourself.

## 4. Test — locally

Keep the inner loop native and fast (`cargo check`, `go test ./...`, `pnpm test`); it is for
iteration only. Evidence is the repository's **canonical verdict**: its full test suite or
Bazel target set, run locally in this worktree before anything leaves it. End-to-end tests
run locally too. A red canonical verdict is fixed here, before `/open-pr`.

Before the canonical verdict, while the branch has never been pushed, rebase it onto the
development branch's latest state (`git fetch origin "$dev"`, then `git rebase "origin/$dev"`),
resolve any conflicts here, and check that what the development branch changed still fits this
change, so every later step reads the head that will merge.

With the canonical verdict green and the work committed, run the
[implementation review](references/implementation-review.md): Codex reads the change against the
ticket, for defects, and against the repository's standards, the code smells and the module
principles, each separately. Decide on its findings once, and run the canonical verdict again
after any fix.

## 5. Tick, and write the ticks back

Every checklist line now carries its file and its test. Edit the ticket's checklist comment,
the one `/claim` posted, to match, and stamp it with the head SHA:

```markdown
<!-- ic:checklist head=<sha> -->
## Requirements checklist · /ic · <ISO time>
- [x] R1 <requirement> — verify: test — file: src/x.rs — test: tests/x.rs::r1_…
- [x] R2 …
Canonical verdict: <command> · green · <ISO time>
```

For frontend tasks, also add a `## UI text checks` section to `.ic/checklist.md` and
mirror it in the **same ticket checklist comment**, stamped with the implementation head:

```markdown
## UI text checks
Head: <sha>
| Surface / state | Evidence or way to reach it | Decision / expected visible result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <affected surface and state> | <source or reproduction steps> | <copy and presentation decision> |
Unresolved facts: <none, or what still needs verification>
```

Include the relevant empty, error, permission and partial-data states identified during
implementation, even when the decision is to keep their wording. Backend-only tasks do
not add this section. This section is the record `/acceptance` reads after a resume or a
checkout on another machine.

`/ready-for-review` reads this comment as one of its three conditions; a checklist ticked
only on one machine is a checklist nobody else can trust.

## Handing off

Echo, for the caller: the worktree path, the branch, the head SHA, the changed files, and the
canonical command that went green. `/acceptance` takes it from here when the ticket has a
surface a person can see or declares evidence; when it has neither, `/open-pr` does.
For frontend work, also identify the UI text checks section and its head in the local
checklist and ticket comment so the next step can retrieve it. The worktree, the commits and
the checklist comment are this step's record.

## Not this

- Reading the ticket and writing the checklist → `/claim`.
- Verifying the machine → `/readiness`.
- Screenshots and the acceptance report → `/acceptance`. The PR → `/open-pr`.

44	principles — shallow interfaces, pass-throughs that fail the deletion test, seams with a single

48	The code smells are a fixed baseline from Fowler's Refactoring, chapter 3, and apply even where
49	the repository documents nothing. A documented repository standard always wins: where it
50	endorses something a smell would flag, the smell is suppressed. Each smell is a labelled
51	judgement call ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation. Each reads what it is, then
52	how to fix it:
53	
54	- Mysterious Name: a function, variable or type whose name does not reveal what it does or
55	  holds. → Rename it; when no honest name comes, the design is murky.
56	- Duplicated Code: the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file of the change.
57	  → Extract the shared shape, call it from both.
58	- Feature Envy: a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → Move the
59	  method onto the data it envies.
60	- Data Clumps: the same few fields or parameters keep travelling together, a type wanting to be
61	  born. → Bundle them into one type, pass that.
62	- Primitive Obsession: a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its
63	  own type. → Give the concept its own small type.
64	- Repeated Switches: the same switch or if-cascade on the same type recurs across the change.
65	  → Replace it with polymorphism, or with one map both sites share.
66	- Shotgun Surgery: one logical change forces scattered edits across many files of the diff.
67	  → Gather what changes together into one module.
68	- Divergent Change: one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → Split it so
69	  each module changes for one reason.
70	- Speculative Generality: abstraction, parameters or hooks added for needs the ticket does not
71	  have. → Delete it; inline it back until a real need shows.
72	- Message Chains: a long a.b().c().d() navigation the caller should not depend on. → Hide the
73	  walk behind one method on the first object.
74	- Middle Man: a class or function that mostly delegates onward. → Cut it, call the real target

# Implementation review — a second model reads the change against the ticket

Run after §4's canonical verdict is green and the work is committed, before §5. Codex reviews
what this branch adds over the development branch, on three separate questions: **does it do
what the ticket asks**, **does it hold up when it runs**, and **is it well-built code**. The
review informs; the implementing session decides what to change, and nothing here blocks the
run. Everything it writes stays in `.ic/`; it posts nothing to the ticket or the PR.

## 1. Assemble the prompt

The model is the first line that is neither blank nor a comment of
[codex-models.txt](../../review-pr/references/codex-models.txt). Write the prompt to
`.ic/implementation-review.prompt.txt`, in this order:

1. The instructions below, verbatim.
2. **The ticket** — its description, acceptance criteria and `.ic/checklist.md`, as `/claim` read
   them.
3. **The repository's standards** — `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and whatever
   coding rules they point at, each under its own path.
4. **The module principles** — [codebase-design/SKILL.md](../../codebase-design/SKILL.md), in
   full.
5. **The complete diff** — `git diff "$(git merge-base HEAD "origin/$dev")"...HEAD`, never cut
   or excerpted.

files beyond what is here; review only, and start no other agent. Everything after these

did not ask for; (c) requirements that look done but are done wrong. Quote the ticket or
checklist line for each.

## Defects
Defects the change introduces: correctness, security, data loss, concurrency, API and
behavioural contract violations, missing error handling. Grade each Critical, High, Medium or
Low, give the failure scenario, and do not claim one without tracing the relevant path.

## Code quality
(a) breaches of the repository's documented standards, citing the file and the rule; (b) the
code smells below; (c) modules that break the module
principles — shallow interfaces, pass-throughs that fail the deletion test, seams with a single
adapter, tests that reach past the interface. Skip what the repository's tooling already
enforces.

The code smells are a fixed baseline from Fowler's Refactoring, chapter 3, and apply even where
the repository documents nothing. A documented repository standard always wins: where it
endorses something a smell would flag, the smell is suppressed. Each smell is a labelled
judgement call ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation. Each reads what it is, then
how to fix it:

- Mysterious Name: a function, variable or type whose name does not reveal what it does or
  holds. → Rename it; when no honest name comes, the design is murky.
- Duplicated Code: the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file of the change.
  → Extract the shared shape, call it from both.
- Feature Envy: a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → Move the
  method onto the data it envies.
- Data Clumps: the same few fields or parameters keep travelling together, a type wanting to be
  born. → Bundle them into one type, pass that.
- Primitive Obsession: a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its
  own type. → Give the concept its own small type.
- Repeated Switches: the same switch or if-cascade on the same type recurs across the change.
  → Replace it with polymorphism, or with one map both sites share.
- Shotgun Surgery: one logical change forces scattered edits across many files of the diff.
  → Gather what changes together into one module.
- Divergent Change: one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → Split it so
  each module changes for one reason.
- Speculative Generality: abstraction, parameters or hooks added for needs the ticket does not
  have. → Delete it; inline it back until a real need shows.
- Message Chains: a long a.b().c().d() navigation the caller should not depend on. → Hide the
  walk behind one method on the first object.
- Middle Man: a class or function that mostly delegates onward. → Cut it, call the real target
  directly.
- Refused Bequest: a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it

# TXE-3764 formatMoney displays zero-decimal and three-decimal currencies incorrectly, and negative number format is wrong

`formatMoney` treats all currencies as having two decimal places: `formatMoney(1234, 'JPY')` displays `¥12.34`, but should be `¥1,234`; `formatMoney(1234567, 'KWD')` displays `KD12,345.67`, but should be `KD1,234.567`. The Japanese yen, Korean won and Kuwaiti dinar amounts in customer emails are all wrong.

Also, negative numbers display as `$-19.99`, but finance requires `-$19.99`; unsupported currencies throw `Cannot destructure property 'symbol'`, which doesn't show which currency it is.

Please fix `src/format.js`; currency decimal places are based on `src/currencies.js`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decimal places come from the `decimals` of that currency in `src/currencies.js`: `formatMoney(1234, 'JPY')` gives `¥1,234`, `formatMoney(1234567, 'KWD')` gives `KD1,234.567`, `formatMoney(5, 'KWD')` gives `KD0.005`; output for two-decimal currencies stays unchanged.
- [ ] The minus sign of negative numbers goes before the currency symbol: `formatMoney(-1999, 'USD')` gives `-$19.99`.
- [ ] Amounts within `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` display exactly: `formatMoney(900719925474099, 'USD')` is `$9,007,199,254,740.99`.
- [ ] Unsupported currencies throw `RangeError`, and the message includes the currency code; when `amountMinor` is not a safe integer, throw `TypeError`.
- [ ] New unit tests cover the above behavior, and `npm test` passes.

# /open-pr — a draft PR whose body says why, what, and how it was proven

**Spec (authority):** Obsidian `Project Magi/Workflow/Specs/Session/IC Session.md` (WF-IC — the
corpus has no separate node for this step), with the *PR* row of
`Project Magi/Workflow/System Design.md` §2 and WFR-007 (one ticket, one merge; the closing
trailer in the body). Where this file and those documents disagree, those documents win: update
this file to match them.

## Contract — what goes in, what comes out

| | |
|---|---|
| **In** | the branch from `/implement` with its head SHA and ticked checklist; the acceptance report URL and inspected screenshots from `/acceptance` when it ran; the ticket |
| **Out** | a **draft** PR against the development branch, body per the template or the six sections, screenshots embedded, `Closes TXE-<n>` for exactly one ticket; the PR URL commented on the ticket; the first review requested |
| **Next** | `/fix-pr`, invoked immediately — then `/ready-for-review` |

## When this skill starts

- **On request:** `/open-pr`, "open the PR", "create a PR for this", "draft the PR body".
- **From `/ic`:** as step 5, after `/implement` and `/acceptance`.
- **Proactively:** the branch is implemented and tested, the checklist is ticked, and no PR
  exists. Say "running /open-pr" and begin.
- **Not** with a red canonical verdict → back to `/implement`. Not with unticked checklist
  lines and no blocking comment on the ticket → back to `/implement`.

## 1. Push

```bash
git push -u origin "$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)"
```

The PR targets the repository's **development branch**, the same one `/implement` cut from:
the integration branch its contract or `CLAUDE.md` names, and when neither names one, the
repository's default branch.

## 2. The body — from the template, or in this order

Review arrives on the PR, CI runs on it and Auto Merge reads it, so its body is the one
document a reviewer, a gate and every later reader all read.

**If the repository has a PR template** (`.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`,
`.github/pull_request_template.md`, or a `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/` directory), follow it
first: fill every section it defines, in its order, and put screenshots in the section it
provides for them. Add the trailer and the acceptance report link where the template has no
home for them, at the end.

**Without a template**, assemble the body in this order — each section present, even when its
content is one line:

1. **Why** — the background, where the requirement came from (the ticket, the brief, the
   incident), how urgent it is, and the problem this solves.
2. **What changed** — the scope of the change and its content: which parts, what behaviour is
   different, what is deliberately untouched.
3. **Before / after** — when there is an end-to-end surface, stitch the before and after
   screenshots into one image with ImageMagick
   (`magick before.png after.png +append compare.png`) so the reviewer sees the difference in
   one look; for a new feature, screenshots that show it working *and* that the neighbouring
   features still do. These come from `/acceptance`. When `command -v magick` prints nothing,
   install ImageMagick 7, the release that provides `magick`, with the machine's package manager
   (`brew install imagemagick` on macOS), then stitch.
4. **Progress** — where the ticket stands after this PR: complete, or which criteria remain
   (from the checklist).
5. **Tests run** — what was executed and where: unit and integration suites, the canonical
   verdict with its command, the acceptance report with its URL.
6. **Open items** — what this PR does not include: the things left out on purpose, and the
   things inside the ticket's scope that were not done here with the follow-up ticket filed
   for each. Nothing is left implicit.

Then the trailer. It goes in the **body** — the surface that is observed to close and stamp
the ticket — and it names exactly one ticket; a bare id without a verb only links the ticket:

```
Closes TXE-<n>
```

## 3. Screenshots, through `gh image`

`gh image` uploads a file and prints the markdown for it; paste that markdown into the section
yourself. List the installed extensions first:

```bash
gh extension list
```

When `drogers0/gh-image` is not in the list, install it:

```bash
gh extension install drogers0/gh-image
```

Then upload each image:

```bash
gh image <compare.png> --repo <owner>/<repo>  # prints the markdown for the body
```

Check the exit status and every returned URL before pasting; a broken image in a PR body is a
reviewer's first impression. A failed upload stops this step with its error.

## 4. Open — as a draft

This skill's working directory is `.open-pr/` in the current directory. Before writing
anything into it, create `.open-pr/.gitignore` containing `*` with the file editing tool.
Then write the body to `.open-pr/body.md` with the file editing tool. Without a template, the
body has this shape:

```markdown
## Why
<background · where the requirement came from · urgency · the problem this solves>

## What changed
<scope and content of the change; what is deliberately untouched>

## Before / after
<markdown returned by gh image: the stitched comparison, or the feature working and its neighbours intact>

## Progress
<complete, or which criteria remain>

## Tests run
- <suite or command> — <result>
- Acceptance: <engapp.dev report URL>

## Open items
- Not in this PR on purpose: <item>
- In scope, not done here: <item — follow-up TXE-<m>>

Closes TXE-<n>
```

Then open the PR with that file as its body:

```bash
gh pr create --draft --base "<dev>" --title "<type>(<scope>): <what changed>" --body-file .open-pr/body.md
```

Open it as a **draft**: `/fix-pr` runs on the draft, and "ready for review" is
`/ready-for-review`'s verdict once every thread is resolved and CI is green. Read the created
PR back once — title, base, body, draft flag — before moving on.

## 5. Tell the ticket, ask for the first review, and go straight to `/fix-pr`

Comment the PR URL on the ticket. Then run `/review-pr` on the PR for its first review: the PR
is a draft, and the PR-polling review service skips drafts.

Then **invoke [fix-pr](../fix-pr/SKILL.md) in the same turn**, which arms the watcher over
this PR. The PR URL is this skill's artifact and the next step's input; it is not a hand-over
to the user, and the review has not arrived yet. Reporting the URL and stopping leaves an
unreviewed draft nobody is watching.

## Not this

- Producing the screenshots and the report → `/acceptance`.
- Waiting for the review, fixing what it finds, fixing a red check → `/fix-pr`.
- Marking ready for review → `/ready-for-review`. Merging → the repository's gate.

input.content:
## Why
TXE-3764: `formatMoney` treated every currency as having two minor-unit digits, so the yen, won and Kuwaiti dinar amounts in customer emails were wrong (`formatMoney(1234, 'JPY')` printed `¥12.34`). Finance also requires the minus sign before the symbol (`-$19.99`). An unsupported currency crashed with `Cannot destructure property 'symbol'`, and the message did not say which currency it was.

## What changed
- `src/format.js`: the number of minor-unit digits comes from `decimals` in `src/currencies.js` (JPY and KRW 0, KWD 3, all others 2). The amount is split into whole and fractional parts on its decimal string, so every amount up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` prints exactly. A negative amount gets `-` before the symbol.
- `formatMoney` throws a `RangeError` whose message is `Unsupported currency: <code>` when the currency is not an own key of `CURRENCIES` (so `'toString'` is rejected too). It throws a `TypeError` when `amountMinor` is not a safe integer (fractions, `NaN`, `Infinity`, strings, `BigInt`, values beyond ±2^53−1).
- `test/format.test.js`: new tests for each of the behaviours above. The four existing two-decimal tests are unchanged and still pass.
- `src/currencies.js`, `src/index.js` and the public signature `formatMoney(amountMinor, currency)` are unchanged.

## Before / after
Output of `formatMoney` on `main` (cad4548) and on this branch:

| call | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `formatMoney(1999, 'USD')` | `$19.99` | `$19.99` |
| `formatMoney(1234, 'JPY')` | `¥12.34` | `¥1,234` |
| `formatMoney(50000, 'KRW')` | `₩500.00` | `₩50,000` |

# /review-pr — one independent review pass, posted, and nothing else

**Spec (authority):** Obsidian `Project Magi/Workflow/Specs/Review/Review PR.md` (WF-RPR).
Where this file and the spec disagree, the spec wins: update this file to match it.

## Names

`/review-pr` invokes this skill. On GitHub its markers carry the name `RPR`: the deduplication
marker, the reply markers and the review attribution. Keep every marker name as it is.
`<!-- OpenAI Codex via RPR -->` is coverage truth for every head reviewed in every repository,
and the detector reviews every head that lacks it, so a renamed marker sends every reviewed head
back through review.

## The gate verdict

This skill writes no merge-ready gate verdict. In `capsohq/txe` the gate (`review-fix`) is a
check-run that a CI workflow writes after reading the posted review. The authority boundary
below forbids statuses outright.

## Authority boundary

Treat this boundary as absolute:

- Post at most one substantive RPR GitHub COMMENT review per exact head SHA.
- In monitored mode, post at most one deduplicated reply per qualifying author
  follow-up event when the head is already reviewed and unchanged.
- Do not edit repository files or generated artifacts.
- Do not commit or push.
- Do not update the PR title, body, labels, reviewers, checks, or commit statuses.
- Do not post a triage response promising fixes. A follow-up reply may answer a
  question, request a pushed commit, or explain review state; it never claims
  that RPR will implement changes.
- Do not merge, close, mark ready, release, or deploy.
- Do not fix findings. Fixing them is `/fix-pr`, the other half of this pair.
- You MAY **create** Linear issues, and only Linear issues, for pre-existing
  findings (§5a). This is the single enumerated write outside the read-only
  posture, and it touches no GitHub object: no PR, branch, status, label, or
  review changes. Creation only: do not update, reassign, relabel, or
  close an existing issue. Everything else in this list still holds absolutely.

For durable deduplication, a review whose `commit_id` equals the current head SHA covers that
head when its body contains `<!-- OpenAI Codex via RPR -->`, `<!-- OpenAI Codex via RPRB -->`
or the visible footer `Review by OpenAI Codex via RPRB`. Emit only the `RPR` marker in new
reviews. When deduplicating author follow-up events, recognize both
`OpenAI Codex via RPR reply-to:` and `OpenAI Codex via RPRB reply-to:` markers, and emit only
the `RPR` reply marker.

Read-only inspection is allowed: repository documentation, Git history, PR metadata, diffs,
existing reviews, and CI results. Avoid commands that may mutate the checkout. Codex itself
uses a read-only sandbox with approvals disabled.

## Execution model

Run each review in a sub-agent that holds the diff and the review context. Give the sub-agent
this complete skill contract, the repository path or name, and the target PR. The coordinating
agent does not repeat the review. When an OS monitor has launched the current process as an
isolated event worker, perform the review in that worker without spawning another outer
worker; inner static-review calls from §3 stay non-delegating.

In monitored mode, the deterministic detector dispatches work as soon as it finds it. It may
spawn one isolated event worker per uncovered PR head or new same-head author follow-up, up to
the worker cap, and it reserves and deduplicates the job identity before spawning. The detector
itself never invokes a model or reviews code while polling.

If the sub-agent fails after the review was posted, inspect GitHub and report the durable
result. If no substantive review was posted, report the failure to the user and stop.

## Workflow

### 1. Resolve the repository and open PR

Use the repository named by the user. Discover a local checkout with `rg --files` or GitHub access when necessary. Resolve the repository identity with:

```bash
gh repo view --json owner,name,defaultBranchRef
```

List only open PRs:

```bash
gh pr list --state open --json number,title,url,headRefName,headRefOid,baseRefName,isDraft
```

Never use an implicit or closed PR. If exactly one PR is open and the user says “the open PR,” review it. If several are open and no target can be inferred safely, ask which one.

Record the PR number, URL, base branch, and exact head SHA. Write this review's files under
`.review-pr/` in the current directory, created with a `.gitignore` containing `*`, and put the
repository, PR number and head SHA in each file name.

### 2. Read project instructions and collect evidence

Read the repository’s applicable `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, code-review guide, workflow contract, and files directly referenced by those instructions. Follow freshness and path-specific rules.

Fetch:

- PR title and body
- complete `base...head` diff
- changed-file list
- relevant helper implementations omitted from small diff hunks
- existing CI/check results
- existing review comments when they materially affect correctness

Do not build, test, format, generate, or otherwise touch the checkout. Cite existing CI results
as evidence of what CI ran; this review establishes correctness.

### 3. Run one Codex review

Resolve the model with `references/codex-model.md` and `references/codex-models.txt`, both of
which ship with this skill.

Write the prompt below to `.review-pr/OWNER_REPO_N_HEAD.prompt.txt`, then run one static
reviewer on it with the resolved model:

```bash
codex exec -m <model> -s read-only -c approval_policy=never -c model_reasoning_effort=high \
  --disable apps --ephemeral --skip-git-repo-check \
  --output-last-message .review-pr/OWNER_REPO_N_HEAD.md < .review-pr/OWNER_REPO_N_HEAD.prompt.txt
```

Embed the complete diff in the prompt. Codex reviews statically from the provided evidence:
tell it that it cannot run commands, fetch GitHub, or read the checkout.
Never use `head`, `tail`, `sed` ranges, line limits, or excerpts to fit a diff.
If the complete evidence exceeds the partition threshold below, partition it with a verified
complete-file manifest; truncation is always a failed review. The review artifact is the file
`--output-last-message` writes; stdout carries diagnostics and is never the review. After
`codex exec` exits, wait up to 30 seconds for that file to have content: the CLI can write it
just after the process ends.

Use a prompt with these requirements:

```text
Review PR #N at PR_URL at exact head HEAD_SHA.

Perform a code review only. Analyze the complete embedded diff for correctness,
security, data loss, concurrency, API/behavioral contract violations, missing
error handling, and adherence to the supplied project conventions. Separate
issues introduced by this PR from pre-existing issues. Do not suggest broad
refactors or style-only changes unless they hide a correctness risk.

For Go changes, inspect context propagation, wrapped/sentinel errors, nil paths,
goroutine/resource cleanup, SQL parameterization, transaction boundaries, and
project logger conventions. Cross-check any API Changes section and referenced
spec/code-path contracts.

Group actionable findings into severity sections in this exact order:
"### Critical [N]", "### High [N]", "### Medium [N]", then "### Low [N]",
where `N` is the exact number of findings in that section. Include only sections
that have findings. Within each section, number findings consecutively from 1,
restarting at 1 for each severity, and give every finding a concise, descriptive
heading in the form "#### 1. Finding title". Do not repeat the severity in each
finding title. For every finding, include a specific file and line or diff hunk,
the failure scenario, and the correct fix. Do not claim a finding without tracing
the relevant path.

For every finding, also include a line reading exactly
"Origin: Introduced by this PR" or "Origin: Pre-existing". Put it inside the
finding body — do not add a section, change the severity grouping, or renumber
anything for it. "Pre-existing" means the defect is already live in the base
branch and would remain after this PR merges.

You cannot run commands or modify files. Return the full review text only.
Header: "## Codex Code Review (MODEL, high)"
Immediately after the header, include exactly one hidden deduplication marker:
"<!-- OpenAI Codex via RPR -->"
Do not include a visible RPR attribution footer or end the review with
"Review by OpenAI Codex via RPR" in any Markdown form.
If there are no actionable findings, say so explicitly and list the areas
checked. Do not say the PR was fixed, merged, or approved.

PROJECT INSTRUCTIONS:
...

PR BODY:
...

COMPLETE DIFF:
...
```

A blank response, a transport error, a request for the diff, or a non-substantive answer is a
failed review: report the failure to the user and post nothing. A stalled response may be
partially rendered, so never triage findings from it; a review truncated before its last
finding reads as complete.

Measure the evidence before invoking Codex. If the assembled prompt exceeds 750 KiB or its
estimated tokens approach 70% of the resolved model's context window, partition the diff
deterministically into coherent complete-file groups, record a manifest proving that every
changed file and hunk is covered, review every group independently with the same model and
effort, then run one final synthesis and deduplication pass. Post nothing unless every group
succeeded and the coverage manifest is complete. The final GitHub artifact is one COMMENT
review for the exact head; chunk outputs stay internal evidence.

Run chunk and synthesis Codex calls as non-delegating inner reviewers. Isolate them from
user-installed skill auto-triggering (for example with a clean Codex home or the supported
ignore-user-config option), and explicitly forbid them from invoking RPR, spawning agents,
fetching GitHub, or posting artifacts. If an inner call attempts to re-enter the outer RPR
workflow, terminate it, accept no output from it, report the failure to the user, and post
nothing.

### 4. Guard against a stale review

Before posting, resolve the PR head SHA again. If it differs from the reviewed SHA, discard the result and review the new exact head. Never knowingly post findings against stale code without labeling them stale.

### 5. Post the review only

Verify `.review-pr/OWNER_REPO_N_HEAD.md`, the review `codex exec` wrote, and post it as a
COMMENT review:

```bash
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/N/reviews -X POST \
  -f event=COMMENT \
  -F body=@.review-pr/OWNER_REPO_N_HEAD.md
```

Codex returns the text and the coordinating agent posts it, because connector review writes may be unavailable. Post the review verbatim. Do not add a second triage review, issue comment, status, or metadata change.

Before posting, verify that the required header and hidden deduplication marker
each occur exactly once, that no visible RPR attribution footer is present,
that the final line contains review content, and that findings are grouped under
descending severity headings. Verify every severity header uses the
`### Severity [N]` form, its bracketed count exactly matches the number of
findings in that section, and its `####` finding headings are numbered
consecutively from 1. Also verify numbering restarts at 1 in each section and no
finding heading repeats its severity label.

### 5a. File a ticket for each pre-existing finding

A finding tagged `Origin: Pre-existing` is a real defect already live in the base branch.
Nobody fixes it in the PR under review, and RPR posts one review and stops, so the finding
gets a Linear ticket that someone will query.

**The procedure lives in `references/follow-up-admission.md`. Follow it verbatim; do not
restate any of it here.** It carries the ladder (leave it in the review → search for an existing
issue → consolidate → admit), the exposure gate that decides filing at every severity, the mandatory
priority, and the ticket body, including how to construct the `Observed evidence` permalink
from the base tree.

**Do not post the filed ids to the PR.** §5's one-review-per-head rule and the authority
boundary both still hold: the review is the only GitHub artifact. The ticket is the durable
record; the user hears about it in step 6.

### 6. Report completion

Tell the user:

- which PR and exact head were reviewed
- whether actionable findings were posted, grouped by severity
- the GitHub review identifier or URL when available
- **every Linear ticket filed under §5a, by id**, and every pre-existing finding that was not
  filed, with the existing issue that already tracks it when there is one
- the writes this run made: the COMMENT review, and the Linear issues filed under §5a

### 7. Monitor and respond to author follow-ups

In monitored mode, watch these events for every eligible open PR:

- `pull_request` opened, reopened, synchronized, or head changed
- `issue_comment` created or edited
- `pull_request_review_comment` created or edited
- `pull_request_review` submitted or edited when it contains author feedback

Process only comments from the PR author that materially respond to RPR,
report a code fix, request re-review, or ask a review-related question. Ignore
RPR's own comments, unrelated chatter, and already handled event identities.
Continue monitoring after every response so author replies are handled
recursively.

For every event, re-fetch the authoritative open/merged state, author, exact
head SHA, reviews, conversation comments, and inline comments. Then choose
exactly one path:

1. **New uncovered head**: reserve `OWNER/REPO#PR@HEAD`, include the relevant
   author follow-ups as review context, and immediately spawn one isolated RPR
   review worker. Post no acknowledgement unless the author asked a separate
   question that the review cannot answer.
2. **Reviewed unchanged head, author asks a question**: post one concise direct
   answer. Reply inline when the source is an inline review comment; otherwise
   reply in the PR conversation. Do not post a second review for the same head.
3. **Reviewed unchanged head, author reports fixes or requests re-review**:
   state that the remote head is still `HEAD` and that a fresh review will run
   after a new commit is pushed. Do not validate local or unpushed claims.
4. **No actionable question, fix claim, or new head**: post nothing.

Deduplicate replies using the source type, comment/review ID, and `updated_at`.
Include exactly one hidden raw-body marker in each reply:

```text
<!-- OpenAI Codex via RPR reply-to:SOURCE_TYPE:SOURCE_ID:UPDATED_AT -->
```

Do not show a visible RPR attribution. Before posting, confirm no existing
reply contains the same event marker. After posting, fetch the durable comment
or inline reply and verify its body and target thread directly.

Post PR-conversation replies with:

```bash
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/issues/N/comments -X POST -F body=@REPLY_FILE
```

Post inline replies with:

```bash
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/N/comments -X POST \
  -F in_reply_to=SOURCE_COMMENT_ID -F body=@REPLY_FILE
```

### 8. Self-heal monitored mode without idle model usage

Do not keep a model-backed monitor, coordinator, or watchdog alive. Use the
SQLite-backed deterministic detector in `scripts/review_monitor.py`, supervised
by the OS (for example, `launchd`). The detector polls GitHub, debounces exact
heads, preflights the complete diff, persists leases, circuits, attempts and
usage, writes heartbeats, and consumes no Codex quota while it polls. GitHub's
exact-head marker is completion truth; SQLite is the local operational control
plane.

**Do not hand-write the supervisor.** `wf` owns provisioning, because every path in a launchd
job is machine-specific — `uv`, `gh`, `codex`, the script, the state directory — and a
hand-written plist is how a working monitor becomes a machine that silently reviews nothing:

```bash
wf review-pr install --repo txehq/tokun-cn   # resolve paths, write the plist, load the job
wf review-pr status                            # per repo: loaded, last heartbeat
wf review-pr logs --repo txehq/tokun-cn      # where the supervisor writes, and the tail
wf review-pr uninstall --repo txehq/tokun-cn # unload and remove; state is left in place
```

`install` resolves `uv`, `gh`, `codex` and `node` the way `/readiness` does — login shell,
session, then a minimal environment. The detector receives `uv`, `gh` and `codex` as absolute
paths, because launchd runs with a `PATH` that resolves almost nothing, and the job's `PATH`
holds the directories of all four for the workers: npm's `codex` runs `#!/usr/bin/env node`,
and a follow-up worker runs `gh`. The job runs the detector with `uv run --script`, which
installs the dependency the script declares (`markdown-it-py`). `install` refuses when any of
the four is missing, and refuses a repository `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO` cannot read with the
current GitHub credentials: a monitor that installs cleanly and then cannot poll is the failure
this command exists to prevent.

**An open circuit is cleared with the detector's own flag.** A failed job opens a durable
circuit, and only an explicit exact-job reset clears it. Read the job's `last_error` before
resetting it. Reset keeps the attempt and token history; a review job gets a fresh preflight,
and a follow-up job is dispatched again. The detector holds a single-instance lock, so unload
the job, run the reset, and install the job again:

```bash
wf review-pr uninstall --repo OWNER/REPO
uv run --script <script> --repo OWNER/REPO --state-dir <dir> --reset-job 'OWNER/REPO#PR@HEAD' --once
wf review-pr install --repo OWNER/REPO
```

`<script>` is `bundle/skills/review-pr/scripts/review_monitor.py` under `wf`'s active
generation, and `<dir>` is the state directory `wf review-pr install` printed.

One supervised process per repository. That is the isolation boundary in the detector —
leases, circuits and the database are per state directory — and `install` keeps it.

**`status` reads the heartbeat.** The detector writes `heartbeat.json` after each validated
poll, and a wedged detector stops writing it while its process stays alive.

For an uncovered exact head, launch one ephemeral strongest-model/high-reasoning
static reviewer directly. Stream the complete prompt on stdin, capture only
`--output-last-message`, validate the review structure with a Markdown parser,
re-fetch the exact head and deduplication marker, then post and verify one
COMMENT review deterministically. If a valid review contains a pre-existing
Medium+ finding, open the circuit for manual Linear triage before posting. After
filing the §5a tickets, post the held review with the §5 command: it is
`jobs-v2/<job>.attempt-<n>.review.md` in the state directory, where `<job>` is the
job id with `/`, `#` and `@` written as `_`. The next poll sees the head covered
and completes the job.
Launch an ephemeral `gpt-5.6-luna` low-reasoning worker only for semantic author
follow-ups; do not nest a Sol CLI process inside Luna for ordinary review jobs.

Apply these recovery rules:

- Run at most one job per durable identity: `OWNER/REPO#PR@HEAD` for reviews and
  `SOURCE_TYPE:SOURCE_ID:UPDATED_AT` for replies. Permit concurrent jobs for
  distinct PRs up to the configured worker cap.
- A worker that exits with a non-zero code, a reviewer that leaves no final-message
  artifact, and a review that fails structure validation each open a durable
  circuit for the job. No job is retried: only an explicit exact-job reset clears a
  circuit, and reset keeps attempt and token history, runs a fresh deterministic
  preflight for a review job, and dispatches a follow-up job again.
- The circuit opens before a review is posted: a detector that stops mid-post
  never posts the review twice, a verified post completes the job, and the next
  poll completes a job whose head GitHub shows covered.
- Preflight outcomes are recorded states: a closed, draft or own PR, or one that
  changes no files, is ineligible; a covered head completes its job; a diff
  GitHub will not serve, or one above the single-review limit, opens the circuit
  for a chunked review with `/review-pr`. A cancelled or stale job whose head
  returns is preflighted again.
- Workers run in their own process group, so a detector restart leaves them
  running and the next process reaps them.
- An unexpected error — a GitHub error, invalid JSON, an empty diff for a PR that
  changes files, corrupted evidence — ends the detector process, and the OS
  restarts it. On startup,
  acquire the single-instance file lock, reconstruct all eligible PRs from
  GitHub, reconcile dead leases, and baseline historical author comments. Jobs
  found in a `state.json` state file are imported with their circuits open.
- Emit a heartbeat after each validated poll and persist reservations before
  dispatch. Use exact-head reviews and reply markers on GitHub as the source of
  truth after any restart.
- Reap completed workers, and discard jobs whose head changed or whose PR closed.
- Keep worker sessions ephemeral and logs file-backed. Never invoke a model for
  heartbeat checks, ordinary polling, queue management, or process recovery.
- Run daily retention only while idle: preserve active jobs and their evidence,
  compact usage aggregates, expire detailed attempts, events and evidence by
  policy, checkpoint WAL, incrementally vacuum, and pause dispatch at the
  database-size guard.

The detector's tests run from the repository root and need an authenticated `gh` and the
`codex` CLI:

```bash
uv run --with 'markdown-it-py>=3' python -m unittest discover -s skills/review-pr/scripts -p 'test_*.py'
```

The detector and OS supervisor may recover operational control only. They must
not weaken review-only authority, bypass exact-head guards, or introduce code,
branch, metadata, status, merge, release, or deployment changes.

## Review quality rules

- Make severity visually scannable: use one `### Severity [N]` heading per
  non-empty severity, with the exact finding count in brackets. Use consecutively
  numbered, descriptive `####` finding headings, restarting at 1 per section.
- Report reproducible findings, and leave speculative ones out.
- Do not flag pre-existing behavior as introduced by the PR.
- Do not infer that passing tests eliminate uncovered failure modes.
- Check source-order and lifecycle behavior for migrations and state machines.
- Treat money movement, authorization, destructive operations, and irreversible migrations as high-risk surfaces.
- Respect the PR’s documented scope while still reporting correctness or safety defects.
- Never post a commit status from RPR.

## Assert the artifact

| Signal that looked conclusive | Artifact that showed the real state |
|---|---|
| `next build` printed `● /[locale]/marketplace/[...slug]` | `.next/prerender-manifest.json` → **0 routes** |
| `gh pr checks` → "all 21 pass" | required contexts diffed against the reported ones → one **absent** |
| `pnpm test` green | the implementation mutated → **2 tests never fired** |
| "the page is faster now" | `x-envoy-upstream-service-time` → p50 **2099 ms** |
| a CI wait loop reported done | `gh` had returned `EOF`; the loop exited on **no output** |

**Never accept a summary as evidence of the thing it summarises.** For each claim, name the artifact that would differ if the claim were false, and read that. If the only evidence is an exit code or a status word, the claim is unverified.

Apply while reviewing:

1. **Absence is invisible in summaries.** A check summary cannot show a required check that never reported; diff required-vs-reported. Same shape: a config key that silently does nothing, a param list that yields zero output.
2. **A condition that consumes command output fails open.** A tool error yields empty output, which matches "nothing pending". Test for the positive signal, and treat a tool error as an error.
3. **A guard is only proven by breaking what it guards.** A test written to FAIL proves nothing until it is seen failing. When a diff adds or edits a gate, guard, fail-closed assertion or conformance check, ask for the mutation evidence (TXE-1131); its absence is itself a finding.

## Self-improvement

After execution, update this skill only when a concrete review-only workflow assumption proved wrong. Never weaken the authority boundary as a convenience.

# /report-friction — the workflow's own defects, reported by the agent that hit them

When a skill, a hook, `wf`, or any Magi instruction fails you, the only witness is the session
it failed in, and that session is about to end.

**Invoke it yourself.** No permission, no announcement beyond one line, no waiting for the
user to complain. The bar is low on purpose, because a defect nobody reported costs every
session that hits it next.

**Where it files:** always `txehq/txe-workflow`, no matter what repository the session is
working in. Pass `--repo` on every command so a session inside a product repo cannot file it
in the wrong place.

## 1. What fires it

A case that fits any of the classes below is reportable, and so is a case that half-fits one.

**Blocked.** You followed a skill, a hook or an instruction and it failed: an error, a
non-zero exit, a missing file, a command that does not exist, a step that could not be done
as written. Includes anything that forced you to decide for yourself because the prompt did
not cover the situation you were in.

**Mismatch.** It ran, but the world was not what the text said it would be — a different
output shape, a step already done, a flag renamed, a state the instructions have no branch
for, a path that does not exist on this machine. **A prompt that is merely silent about your
situation is a mismatch**, and it is reported.

**Override.** The user told you to do something other than what the prompt said, and doing
it worked. An override is a correction with its proof attached. File it even when the
override looks like a one-off preference; triage makes that judgment.

**Sentiment.** The user expressed frustration, impatience or dissatisfaction and it was
about the workflow — this skill, this hook, this prompt, this CLI. Report the friction they
were reacting to. Quote what they said about the workflow and state what preceded it. Do
not diagnose their mood, do not characterize them, and do not quote anything that is not
about the workflow.

**Install and authentication: report everything.** During `/install`, `/install-manager`,
`wf install`, or any credential or OAuth step: every error, every attempt that did not work,
every instruction from the user that differed, and every path that worked — including a path the skill *did* describe, confirmed working on this
machine, and including a path the skill describes that **failed**, with its exact error.
Installs are run once per machine by someone with no context, so the experience of the run
is the finding.

## 2. Never let the report cost the work

The report is a side effect. It does not pause the task, does not ask a question, and does
not become the subject of the conversation. One line to the user — `filed the /implement
worktree failure as txe-workflow#N` — and back to what you were doing.

**Fire when the case has an outcome**: whether you got past it, how you got past it, and what
the user said are most of the report's value, and a report filed mid-struggle has none of
them. If you move on with the case still open, file it anyway and say plainly that it is
unresolved.

**Do not batch.** One case, one issue. Two unrelated defects in one issue get triaged as
one, and the second one is the one that gets lost.

When a `gh` command fails, the filing stops with that error. A body file already written
stays in its case directory under `.report-friction/`; name it and the error to the user in
one line, and go back to the task.

## 3. Search before you file

The session that hit this before you probably filed it.

```bash
gh issue list --repo txehq/txe-workflow --state all --label friction \
  --search "<the symptom in three or four words>" --limit 20
```

Search the **symptom** in the words the tool printed, for example `worktree already exists`.

- **Same case, issue open** → add a comment. A second machine, a second OS, a different
  error text or a working path the issue does not have is new evidence and belongs on the
  existing thread.
- **Same case, issue closed** → if your evidence contradicts the close or the defect is back,
  reopen it and say why in the same breath. If the close was right and yours is a different
  case wearing similar words, open a new issue and link the old one. **Both are yours to
  decide. Do not ask the user, and do not let a closed issue talk you out of a report.**
- **Nothing similar** → new issue.

## 4. What the report has to carry

The sections and their order are those of the repository's own
[friction-report template](https://github.com/txehq/txe-workflow/blob/main/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/friction-report.md),
the one a human filing by hand uses, so both kinds of report are triaged the same way.

1. **What happened.** The exact error, verbatim and in a code block, with the command that
   produced it and the step of the skill you were on. A paraphrase makes a report
   untriageable: *"it failed to find the branch"* cannot be searched for, grepped for, or
   matched against a fix.
2. **The path that worked.** What you actually did to get past it — the commands, in order.
   If nothing worked, say so and say where you stopped. **This is the half that turns a
   complaint into a patch**, and it is the half most often left out.
3. **Why you think it happened.** Your hypothesis, labelled as a hypothesis and kept in its
   own section. State the observation and the guess in separate sentences. A useful
   hypothesis is falsifiable: "The instruction assumes a fresh worktree; this session was
   already in one."
4. **The user's instruction**, verbatim, when there was one, side by side with what the
   prompt said. The wording *is* the finding.
5. **Where it happened.** Version and machine, read from these commands:

```bash
wf status
wf --version
uname -s
```

When `uname -s` prints `Darwin`, run `sw_vers -productVersion`; on any other system, run
`uname -a`.

Name the skill or command and the release that was live. A report against an unknown
version cannot be closed by a fix.

**Redact before you paste.** No tokens, no API keys, no `Authorization:` headers, no
`.env` contents; text you paste by hand passes through no masking. Trim paths and repository
content to what the defect needs: the report is about the workflow, so a product repo's
source does not belong in it.

## 5. File it

This skill's working directory is `.report-friction/` in the current directory. Before writing
anything into it, create `.report-friction/.gitignore` containing `*` with the file editing
tool. Each case gets its own directory, `.report-friction/<case>/`, where `<case>` is the
symptom in lowercase words joined by hyphens. Write the body to
`.report-friction/<case>/body.md` with the file editing tool: a file keeps backticks, newlines
and quoting intact, and a mangled error text is a useless error text.

```bash
gh issue create --repo txehq/txe-workflow \
  --title "[friction] /implement — worktree step fails when the session is already in one" \
  --label friction --label friction:blocked \
  --body-file .report-friction/worktree-step-fails-inside-a-worktree/body.md
```

Title as `[friction] <surface> — <one-line symptom>`, where the surface is the thing at
fault: `/implement`, `wf install`, `hooks/session-start`, `/install (Linear auth)`. The
symptom is what someone would search for.

Add exactly one class label from this list:

| label | the case |
|---|---|
| `friction:blocked` | it failed outright |
| `friction:mismatch` | it ran, and reality did not match the text |
| `friction:override` | the user's different instruction is what worked |
| `friction:sentiment` | the user pushed back on the workflow itself |
| `friction:install` | anything in install, reinstall or authentication |

`friction:install` wins when a case is both. When a label does not exist on the repository,
`gh` rejects the whole call; that error stops the filing like any other `gh` failure (§2).

## 6. Keep it current

The issue is not finished when you file it. Within the same session or a later one:

```bash
gh issue comment <n> --repo txehq/txe-workflow --body-file .report-friction/<case>/comment.md
gh issue edit <n> --repo txehq/txe-workflow --body-file .report-friction/<case>/body.md
gh issue reopen <n> --repo txehq/txe-workflow
```

Write each comment or corrected body into the case's directory with the file editing tool
before passing it. Comment when something new happens — the workaround failed later, the
real cause turned up, it reproduced on another machine. Edit the body when what you filed is
**wrong**, so the issue states the correct facts. Do not comment about the correction. Reopen
when a closed defect comes back.

All of this happens without asking. Interrupting the user to ask permission to file a bug
report is the friction this skill exists to remove.

## What this skill is most likely to get wrong

**Reporting the product's bug in the workflow's tracker.** The test is narrow: would this
still have happened if the skill's text, the hook, or `wf` were different? If yes, it belongs
in the tracker of the repository you are working in.

**Filing the feeling.** A report whose body is *"the install flow is confusing"* cannot be
fixed. The error text, the command, and the step are the report.

**Under-reporting an override because it felt like a preference.** You are not the triage.
File it.
